To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the MAX-DOAs measurements show that the NO 2 concentration is strongly inhomogeneous over the shipping lane.
the onion-peeling approach allows to derive approximate plume positions and in-plume NO 2 VMR from MAX-DOAS observations.

we developed and applied a novel method to derive two-dimensional plume distributions from MAX-DOAS data and that the derived plume positions and NO2 volume mixing ratio agree well with airborne measurements.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a new methodology based on MAX-DOAS observations for investigating the strong horizontal variability of NO2 in the vicinity of a shipping lane and the validation of this method with airborne measurements.
the study of the horizontal distribution of NO2 in the vicinity of the main shipping route to the port of Hamburg.
the study of the horizontal in-homogeneity in NO 2 concentration above a ship lane by using MAX-DOAS technique.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the onion-peeling technique applied to MAX-DOAS observations of shipping emissions is able to provide a good estimate for the position and the in-plume NO 2 VMR.
the presented approach is able to detect and characterize ship emission plumes in the horizontal plane.

the onion-peeling technique is a powerful tool to study the horizontal inhomogeneity of NO2 in shipping plumes and to estimate the plume position in the observed area, but the results should be interpreted with care, especially when the plume is not centered between the two MAX-DOAS channels, as the plume center position can be overestimated by up to 1 km in the case of a 1 km plume width.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a novel approach to study the horizontal distribution of ship plumes using MAX-DOAS, which is validated using airborne measurements.
MAX-DOAS can be used to derive NO2 VMRs and plume positions in shipping plumes.
MAX-DOAS observations of shipping emissions can be used to derive the approximate location of the plumes and the in-plume NO VMRs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the MAX-DOAs technique has the potential to detect NO2 plumes several kilometers away from a measurement site.
the MAX-DOAs technique can provide a unique tool to investigate the horizontal inhomogeneity of shipping emissions in the marine boundary layer and to estimate NO2 VMRs in the plume.
MAX-DOAS can be applied to monitor ship emissions in a very effective way, especially in cases where in-situ measurements are not feasible due to unfavorable wind conditions or other reasons.
